interviewQuestions.question: Explain how quicksort works and why its worst case is O(n²) despite averaging O(n log n).
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Quicksort picks a **pivot**, partitions the array so everything smaller ends up left of it and everything larger ends up right of it — placing the pivot in its final sorted position in the process — then recurses on the two sides. Unlike merge sort, all the real work happens during partitioning, in place, before the recursive calls, so there's no merge step and no extra array.

The complexity hinges entirely on how balanced each split is, and that depends on the pivot. If every partition splits the array roughly in half, you get the same log n depth argument as merge sort: O(log n) levels times O(n) partition work per level equals **O(n log n)**.

The worst case happens when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element in its range — a fixed last-element pivot on an already-sorted array does exactly this every single call, producing a 1-vs-(n−1) split. That gives recursion depth n instead of log n, with O(n) work at each of n levels: **O(n²)**.

The practical fix is randomizing the pivot (or median-of-three): it doesn't make the bad case impossible, but it makes it so improbable for any given input that the *expected* running time is O(n log n) regardless of what the data looks like, and no attacker can construct an input that reliably triggers the bad case since the pivot depends on runtime randomness, not the data.

**Testing:** whether you can connect pivot choice to split balance to complexity, rather than reciting "average case n log n, worst case n squared" without explaining why.

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between Lomuto and Hoare partitioning, and which would you actually implement?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Both rearrange an array around a pivot, but they make different guarantees about the result. Lomuto uses one boundary index that grows as it scans, and finishes with the **pivot placed exactly at the returned index** — everything before is ≤ pivot, everything after is >. Hoare uses two pointers converging from opposite ends and finishes with a valid **partition boundary**, but the pivot's value isn't necessarily sitting at that index — it can be anywhere in either resulting region.

That difference has real consequences. Lomuto swaps on every element found less than the pivot, while Hoare only swaps when both a left and right element are provably misplaced — about **3x fewer swaps** on average, which matters on large arrays. Lomuto also degrades to O(n²) on **all-duplicate arrays** specifically, since its `< pivot` check never fires and the pivot lands at an extreme every time; Hoare's opposite-end approach still splits duplicates roughly evenly.

If I'm asked to write quicksort under interview time pressure, I'd reach for **Lomuto** — it's easier to state correctly and prove to an interviewer live, and the recursive bounds (`p-1`, `p+1`) are simpler to get right. If performance genuinely matters — a production sort, or a dataset likely to have many duplicates — I'd use **Hoare**, being careful to recurse on `[lo, p]` and `[p+1, hi]`, not Lomuto's bounds.

**Testing:** whether you know these are genuinely different algorithms with different guarantees, not two names for the same thing.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: You inherit a quicksort implementation that always uses the first element as pivot. What's wrong with it, and how would you fix it in production?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The problem is that the pivot's quality depends entirely on the data, and a fixed first-element pivot is adversarial against two extremely common input shapes: **already-sorted** and **reverse-sorted** data, both of which show up constantly in practice — re-sorting logs, appending to a maintained-sorted structure, data that arrived pre-sorted from an upstream system. On either shape, every partition produces a maximally unbalanced split, giving O(n²) time and, just as importantly, **O(n) recursion depth**, which can stack-overflow before it even finishes slowly.

The fix doesn't require changing the partition logic at all — just the input to it. Before partitioning, **swap a pivot chosen by randomization or median-of-three into the first (or last) position**, then run the exact same fixed-position partition code unchanged. Randomization gives an expected O(n log n) regardless of input shape, since no fixed array can be adversarial against a pivot chosen at runtime.

I'd also add the **recurse-into-the-smaller-side-first** discipline alongside this: after any partition, compare the two side lengths and recurse (or loop) into the smaller one first. That caps recursion depth at O(log n) even on a split that's uneven but not the true worst case, which the pivot fix alone doesn't guarantee.

In code review I'd flag the fixed pivot immediately — it's a one-line fix with an outsized correctness and reliability payoff, and it's exactly the kind of thing that passes small unit tests and then times out or crashes on a production-sized sorted input.

**Testing:** whether you can diagnose a subtle production bug from first principles and propose the minimal fix, not just "quicksort is fast, ship it."

interviewQuestions.question: Quicksort is described as "in-place," but people say its space complexity is O(log n), not O(1). Why?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
"In-place" refers to the **data** — quicksort rearranges the array by swapping elements within it, never allocating a second array the way merge sort does. But "in-place" and "zero extra memory" aren't the same claim, and the gap is the **call stack**.

Every recursive call to quicksort needs its own stack frame to hold its local variables (the `lo`/`hi` bounds, at minimum) until it returns, and those frames pile up while a call is waiting on its recursive children. With a good pivot strategy, recursion depth is O(log n), so the stack itself uses O(log n) space even though the array being sorted never needed a second copy.

This is exactly why the **recurse-into-the-smaller-half-first** discipline matters as more than a nice-to-have: without it, an implementation that always recurses left-then-right can have its stack depth blow up to O(n) on an unbalanced-but-not-catastrophic split, even while a randomized pivot keeps the *time* complexity fine on average. Depth and average-case time are separate guarantees, and only one of them is fixed by pivot randomization alone.

A true O(1)-auxiliary-space sort has to eliminate recursion entirely — an iterative quicksort using an explicit stack still pays the same O(log n) (or worse, unbounded, if not managed) for that stack; only algorithms like heapsort get genuine O(1) auxiliary space with no stack cost at all.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish "in-place" (no second copy of the data) from "O(1) space" (nothing extra at all), a distinction most candidates blur.
